newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Minority shareholder sues Samsung.
newsitem.headline: Minority shareholder sues Samsung.

text.p: Samsung Electronics Co has been hit by a minority shareholder lawsuit in what analysts said on Wednesday was another indication that South Korean investors were exercising their ownership rights.
Jang Ha-sung, an economics professor at Korea University, filed a lawsuit in a Suwon District Court on Tuesday, seeking to nullify privately placed convertible bonds by Samsung Electronics.
The minority shareholder with just 130 shares in Samsung accused the company of damaging rights for small investors.

"The largest shareholder was arrogant to ignore small investors and gave a damage to them by diluting the value of stock prices," said Jang, who also chairs a civic organisation called People's Solidarity for Participatory Democracy.
The suit involves 60 billion won ($67.59 million) in convertible bonds issued by Samsung Electronics, an affiliate of the powerful Samsung Group, on March 24.
The eldest son of Samsung Group chairman Lee Kun-hee had bought 45 billion won worth of the bonds, while trading arm Samsung Corp had underwritten the rest.
Jang said Samsung issued the bonds at below-market prices. The conversion price was set at 50,000 won. Samsung traded at 56,700 won on March 24, compared with 69,500 on Wednesday.
He said Korean commercial regulations require Samsung to have called for a shareholders meeting to issue the bonds and to give shareholders a priority to underwrite the bonds.
"We have done nothing wrong and followed all laws," said spokesman Cho Jang-won at Samsung Group.
"We cannot understand what kind of damages small investors had specifically experienced. We will wait and see the outcome from the court," Cho said.

Analysts said the lawusit would have no significant impact on Samsung Electronics but that it was another indication that South Korean minority shareholders had awakened to their rights as company owners.
The Samsung suit was preceded by a lawsuit filed in early June by small investors in the Korea First Bank.

Aided by the same civic organisation, a group of minority shareholders representing a 0.5 percent stake of Korea First Bank filed a lawsuit against four former bank executives in connection with loans to failed Hanbo Steel Co.

"It's very desirable for Koreans to comply with the rule of the law," said a lawyer. "Small investors have come to realise that they can stop certain business activities by major shareholders and management."
A common and accepted form of showing dissatisfaction with anything from government to employers in South Korea has been to take to the streets.

"A series of recent lawsuits signalled that companies in Korea will try to focus on maximising interest for shareholders like companies in advanced capitalist countries do," said Kim Min-tae, economist at LG Research Economic Institute.
In Korea, company management which may hold only a five to 10 percent stake tended to view the firm as private property.

Jang said Samsung's action was aimed at transferring ownership to the group chairman's son and asked the court to bar bond holders from exercising their rights or selling the bonds. (Conversion $1 = 887.70)
